title: What if the Baltic states had resisted Stalin?
gist: Gordon F. Sander revisits whether Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania could have resisted the 1940 Soviet takeover as Finland did in the Winter War, concluding resistance was possible but futile militarily, and that the 'myth of Baltic submission' is false. He stresses the question is no longer academic with Baltic-Russian relations at their worst since 1939 and the Baltics on the front line of a new Cold War.

insights.claim: Relations between the Baltic states and Russia are at their lowest point since 1939, with an increasing possibility of a clash, making the question of Baltic resistance no longer academic.
insights.speaker: Gordon F. Sander
insights.so_what: Rising probability of a NATO-Russia flashpoint in the Baltics is a tail risk for European assets and defence spending.
insights.quote: with relations between the Balts and Russia at their lowest point since 1939, and the increasing possibility of a smash-up between the two
insights.locator: Indeed, with relations between the Balts

insights.claim: The Baltic peoples and their rebuilt armies now stand on the front line of a new Cold War with Russia and are prepared to fight for their freedom.
insights.speaker: Gordon F. Sander
insights.so_what: Baltic resolve supports sustained regional defence investment and NATO forward posture.
insights.quote: as they and their rebuilt armies stand on the front line of the new Cold War with Russia

insights.claim: By June 1940 each Baltic state already hosted 20,000-25,000 Soviet troops under 'mutual assistance' treaties, leaving them effectively occupied before the invasion.
insights.speaker: Gordon F. Sander
insights.so_what: Accepting foreign basing under coercion can pre-empt any later ability to resist, a lesson for current small states.
insights.quote: each country had garrisons of 20,000 to 25,000 Soviet troops stationed within their borders, so they were already effectively occupied

insights.claim: Unlike Finland, the Baltic states' short-sighted authoritarian presidents were slow to perceive the Soviet threat and failed to mobilise.
insights.speaker: Gordon F. Sander
insights.so_what: Leadership threat perception and mobilisation readiness matter as much as hardware.

insights.claim: Michael O'Hanlon notes Finland is almost twice the combined size of the three Baltic states and more forested, so Finnish motti tactics would not have worked against Soviet tank armies in the Baltics.
insights.speaker: Gordon F. Sander
insights.so_what: Terrain and strategic depth shape defensibility, explaining why the Baltics depend on NATO reinforcement.
insights.quote: Finland is almost twice the size of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania combined

insights.claim: In June 1940 Latvia had about 30,000 soldiers, 20 tanks, 576 artillery pieces and 172 aircraft; Estonia 15,700 soldiers, 36 tanks, 591 guns and 110 aircraft; Lithuania 28,000 soldiers, 30 tanks, 400 guns and 117 aircraft.
insights.speaker: Gordon F. Sander
insights.so_what: Shows the Baltics were armed enough to resist, so capitulation was a political choice.
insights.locator: To be precise, as of June 1940

insights.claim: Baltic historians Ēriks Jēkabsons and Algimantas Kasparavičius agree military resistance was possible in 1940 but could not have preserved independence, especially after Dunkirk.
insights.speaker: Gordon F. Sander
insights.so_what: Small-state survival depends on the wider great-power context, not just local resistance.

insights.claim: Finland's Winter War, though lost with about 10% of its territory and 25,000 lives, generated lasting moral and inspirational capital, like Thermopylae or the Chosin Reservoir.
insights.speaker: Gordon F. Sander
insights.so_what: Demonstrated will to fight builds national cohesion and external support, relevant for valuing deterrence credibility.
insights.locator: Indeed. In that sense, the Talvisota

insights.claim: Finland squandered its Winter War moral capital in June 1941 by joining Nazi Germany's invasion of the USSR, leading to the disastrous Continuation War.
insights.speaker: Gordon F. Sander
insights.so_what: Revanchist overreach can destroy hard-won international sympathy.
insights.quote: the Finns squandered the moral capital they gained during the Winter War in June 1941

insights.claim: The 1989 Baltic Way, in which two million people linked arms along a 400-mile chain, broke the back of the USSR in the author's view.
insights.speaker: Gordon F. Sander
insights.so_what: Mass civil resistance can accelerate imperial collapse.
insights.quote: It broke the back of the USSR.
insights.locator: Ultimately the Balts did have their finest hour

insights.claim: The myth of unanimous Baltic submission is false: Lithuanian president Antanas Smetona urged resistance and the Estonian Independent Signal Battalion fought Soviet forces in Tallinn on 21 June 1940.
insights.speaker: Gordon F. Sander
insights.so_what: Historical narratives of Baltic passivity understate today's Baltic will to resist.
insights.quote: The myth of Baltic submission was exactly that – a myth.

insights.claim: Stalin used the cover of the fall of Paris to absorb the three Baltic republics on 14-16 June 1940, following the secret protocol of the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact.
insights.speaker: Gordon F. Sander
insights.so_what: Aggressors exploit moments when Western attention is absorbed elsewhere.
